channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: US employers added 165,000 jobs in October against expectations of 65,000, the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% and the CME FedWatch tool puts the chance of a Federal Reserve rate rise on 9 December at 76%.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that US non-farm payrolls rose by 165,000 in October, against market expectations of 65,000 and a revised 60,000 in September, and that the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%. Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% on the month to USD 38 and 3.1% on the year, against 3.0% in September. Yahoo reports gains of 70,000 in professional and business services, 42,000 in healthcare, 25,000 in transportation and warehousing and 19,000 in manufacturing. Lianhe Zaobao cites the CME FedWatch tool at 76% for a 25 basis point rise on 9 December. Chinatimes reports that San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said on 6 November that further tightening is still needed. Associated Press says the October consumer price index is due this week, with economists expecting 3.9% after 3.7% in September. Associated Builders and Contractors counts a net loss of 3,000 construction jobs in October, with nonresidential construction up 13,300; the rows give no split for residential construction. The rows give no revisions for earlier months beyond September.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report labour data and market pricing for a rate rise, not a Federal Reserve decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a strong labour market with wage growth above 3% and inflation expected at 3.9% supports the case for higher rates, and higher rates raise borrowing costs. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, housing and capital goods are sensitive to borrowing costs, so a rate rise could weigh on construction and manufacturing demand in the US, while the added manufacturing and nonresidential construction jobs point to some activity; the rows give no figures for orders. Points that may be worth considering include the October consumer price index, signals from other Federal Reserve officials and mortgage rates.

Commercial Times | Yahoo! | Lianhe Zaobao | Chinatimes | AP | Associated Builders and Contractors

item.title: A sell-off in AI-linked shares cut the S&P 500 by about 4.4% on 5 November and spread to Asia on 6 November, when South Korea's Kospi fell 8.5% and Japan's Nikkei 5.1% in early trading.
item.description:
The Guardian reports that more than USD 3.2 trillion was wiped off the US stock market on 5 November: the S&P 500 lost 4.36%, the Dow fell 1,833.06 points or 3.44% and the Nasdaq tech index fell 5.5%, with memory chip makers falling most. Cnyes reports that the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4%, that the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12% in the day and is 36% below its June high, and that the VIX volatility index rose 11.5 points to 28.09, an eight-month high and its largest one-day rise since the April 2025 tariff announcement. Lianhe Zaobao reports that on 6 November the Kospi fell 8.5% in early trading, halting trading in Seoul for 20 minutes, the Nikkei fell 5.1% in early trading and Taiwan's market and the Nikkei entered a technical bear market, with TSMC down more than 10%. Wallstreet:online reports that the DAX fell about 2%, or nearly 600 points, to 25,717 on 6 November and that it had set a record of 26,685 on 5 November, and that US bond prices fell on Friday as stocks recovered, lifting the 10-year yield to 4.85%. The market commentary in these rows links the sell-off to concern that Democratic control of Congress could slow AI investment and data-centre building; no measure is cited. The rows give no closing levels for Friday in the US and no sector detail beyond chips and large technology shares.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report market moves and the explanations of commentators, not a change in orders or output. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a fall of this size in AI-linked shares can tighten financing for technology firms and raise caution on investment plans, while a rebound within days would limit the effect. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, demand from electronics and semiconductor packaging depends on AI-related investment, and higher volatility can affect financing conditions for customers across manufacturing; the rows give no figures for any of these. Points that may be worth considering include whether markets stabilise this week, announcements on data-centre and chip investment and US measures on AI.

The Guardian | Cnyes.com | Cnyes.com | Lianhe Zaobao | Lianhe Zaobao | Wallstreet:online | Wallstreet:online

item.title: US Central Command said US aircraft bombed the stern of a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman on 7 November for trying to break the blockade of Iran, and a missile is suspected in an attack on a tanker in the Gulf on 5 November that killed a seafarer.
item.description:
Bjd.com.cn reports that US Central Command said US forces struck a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman on 7 November for attempting to violate the US naval blockade of Iran; after the crew was evacuated, US aircraft fired precision-guided bombs at the stern, leaving the ship unseaworthy. According to the announcement, the ship had reportedly attempted to leave the area's waters after docking at an Iranian port, and since July US forces have made 147 merchant ships change course, rendered five unseaworthy and destroyed 10 Iranian tankers. Arab News reports that a seafarer was killed on Thursday in an explosion believed to have been caused by a missile attack on the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Velos Sapphire, which was sailing unladen towards Bahrain; the crew put out a fire, no pollution was reported and the hull damage was still being assessed. China Daily reports that the Iranian Revolutionary Guards say their aerospace division has set up underground missile and drone production sites and is extending missile range, and that the corps is prepared to defend the country "without any geographical limitation" if the enemy renews strikes. The rows do not say who attacked the tanker, give no ship or flow figures for the Gulf of Oman or the Strait of Hormuz, and show no freight, insurance or oil price reaction.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report military incidents and statements, not a measure of shipping or prices. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, attacks on tankers and the enforcement of a blockade raise the risk of operating in Gulf waters and can affect cargo flows and the cost of freight and insurance there. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, petrochemical feedstocks and chemical shipments from or via the region and freight rates feed into raw material costs and delivery times; the rows give no figures for these. Points that may be worth considering include tanker rates and war-risk insurance, further Central Command statements and oil prices at the start of the week.

Bjd.com.cn | Arab News | China Daily

item.title: China's commerce ministry opened anti-dumping investigations on 6 November into para-aramid filament yarn from the EU and into ethylidene norbornene, a chemical used for synthetic rubber, from the EU and Japan.
item.description:
Commercial Times reports that China's Ministry of Commerce opened anti-dumping investigations on 6 November into para-aramid filament yarn from the EU and into ethylidene norbornene (ENB) from the EU and Japan, saying the products are suspected of dumping that damages mainland industries. The import price of para-aramid filament yarn from the EU fell by more than 50% between 2023 and the first half of 2026. For ENB from the EU and Japan, cumulative import volume rose 27.35% from 2023 to 2025 and 56% year on year in the first half of 2026, with import prices trending down. The South China Morning Post says para-aramid yarn is used in optical communications, automotive components, protective equipment and aerospace, and that ENB is mainly used to make synthetic rubber for auto parts, construction materials and other applications. The rows do not say whose figures the price and volume changes are or what the 2023 base is, and give no import values, no names of producers, no provisional duty rates and no timetable for the investigations.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report the opening of investigations, whose outcome is not known. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, such an investigation can lead to provisional duties on the named imports, and it targets imports from the EU and Japan. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, synthetic rubber and high-strength fibres are inputs to sealing, bonding and reinforced products, so duties could change supply routes for producers that use them in China; the rows give no figures for these uses. Points that may be worth considering include the investigation timetable, any provisional duty announcement and reactions from the EU and Japan.

Commercial Times | South China Morning Post

item.title: The German Chamber of Industry and Commerce's innovation report shows that for the first time since the first survey in 2008 more companies in Germany plan to reduce research and development investment than to increase it.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that, according to the new innovation report of the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce (DIHK), more companies in Germany are planning to reduce investment in research and development than to increase it. It is the first time since the first survey in 2008 that more companies have said they plan to cut than to raise R&D investment. The row gives no share of companies for either answer, no sample size or survey date, no split by sector or company size and no reasons given by the companies.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports an intention in a survey, not realised spending. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, plans to cut research and development at customers can reduce the number of new product and process projects in which suppliers take part. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many sales start with development projects at manufacturing customers, so fewer projects could mean fewer new applications to qualify; the row gives no figures by sector. Points that may be worth considering include the sector breakdown in the full report, company statements on development budgets and public research funding in Germany.

Handelsblatt

item.title: UK house prices fell 0.6% in October and were 1.2% below a year earlier, the steepest annual fall since October 2023, the Lloyds index shows, while a Lloyds mortgages director says borrowing costs and renewed inflation weigh on demand.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that the Lloyds house price index shows UK house prices fell 0.6% month on month in October after a 0.1% fall in September, taking the average price to GBP 296,285 from GBP 298,167. On an annual basis prices fell 1.2%, the steepest fall since October 2023, and prices were down 0.5% over the quarter. Lloyds mortgages director Andrew Asaam says elevated borrowing costs and renewed inflationary pressures, linked partly to the Middle East conflict, are weighing on housing demand and household finances. The Independent describes the 1.2% decline as the steepest in three years. The rows give no regional breakdown, no transaction volumes, no mortgage approvals and no data on housebuilding or renovation, and the figure comes from one index.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a price index, which measures house prices and not construction activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, falling prices together with high borrowing costs can reduce the number of new homes started and the willingness of owners to renovate, though the link is indirect and varies by market. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, demand from construction follows new-build and renovation volumes, so a weaker housing market is a possible drag; the rows give no figures for volumes. Points that may be worth considering include other UK price indices, mortgage approval data, housing starts and the direction of interest rates.

MarketScreener | The Independent

item.title: The presidents of Cefic and the VCI demand in a letter to Chancellor Merz fundamental changes to the Commission's emissions trading reform, warning that unchanged it would cut production and jobs and raise import dependence.
item.description:
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports that BASF chief executive Markus Kamieth, as president of the European chemical association Cefic, and Covestro chief executive Markus Steilemann, as president of the German industry association VCI, wrote to Chancellor Friedrich Merz demanding fundamental corrections to the EU Commission's reform proposal for emissions trading. Without them, they write, emissions trading threatens to become an "accelerator of disinvestment and industrial substance loss". They warn that an unchanged proposal would mean less production, fewer jobs, growing dependence on imports and the relocation of emissions to third countries, which would weaken both Europe as a business location and effective climate protection. A separate row from the Spanish chemical federation FEIQUE says it held an information day with the Spanish climate office on the revision of the system for the period after 2030, covering the linear reduction factor, the availability of allowances and the future of free allocation; it gives no positions. The rows do not describe what the Commission's proposal contains, which parts the letter objects to, what the cost effect would be, or when decisions are due.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report an industry letter and a meeting, of which the letter is a statement of position; neither is a decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the allowance price and the amount of free allocation determine the carbon cost of energy-intensive producers such as makers of resins and intermediates, and that cost can be passed on in material prices or lead to lower output in Europe. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, the cost and the location of production of raw materials in Europe affect supply terms and prices, and a rise in imports can change supplier choice; the rows give no figures for these effects. Points that may be worth considering include the Chancellor's response, the timetable of the proposal in the Council and Parliament and positions of other member states and producers.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | FEIQUE

item.title: China's tariff commission will continue to suspend its 24% tariff rate on US goods for two months from 10 November and keep the 10% rate, and US officials told China on 6 November to meet the terms of the Busan truce immediately.
item.description:
China Economic Net reports that the State Council Customs Tariff Commission issued a notice on 9 November adjusting the tariff measures on imports originating in the United States; the notice says the aim is to implement the outcome consensus reached by the heads of state at the Washington meeting. From 13:01 on 10 November China will continue to suspend the 24% tariff rate for two months and retain the 10% rate. On the US side, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer spoke on 6 November with Vice-Premier He Lifeng and raised concerns about China's implementation of the Busan commitments, in particular farm purchases, rare earths and critical minerals, according to the Straits Times, Handelsblatt and Commercial Times. The Financial Times says the Busan truce expires on 10 January 2027. Handelsblatt places the Trump–Xi meeting at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November. Commercial Times, citing Radio Free Asia, and Chinatimes report that China has prepared five trade demands for that meeting, covering tariffs, farm purchases, chip export controls, Chinese investment in the US and cross-border rules. The rows do not say which goods the tariffs cover, which other Chinese tariff measures remain, how the US responded to the notice or how large the rare-earth and farm shortfalls are.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a tariff notice and a warning, not a change in the tariff level. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, continuing a suspension keeps China's current tariff level on US goods in place and leaves the situation open to change when the suspension ends. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, tariffs and export controls on rare earths and other critical minerals can affect the cost and availability of components and raw materials for manufacturing customers in both countries, and the farm-purchase dispute shows how tied the truce is to specific commitments; the rows give no figures for chemicals trade. Points that may be worth considering include the outcome of the APEC meeting, the US reaction to the Chinese notice and data on rare-earth shipments and farm purchases.

China Economic Net | The Straits Times | Handelsblatt | Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Chinatimes | The Financial Times

item.title: German production rose 0.7% in September from August, against an expected stagnation, led by cars up 17.1%, while construction fell 2.6% and mechanical engineering 6.5%, the Federal Statistical Office says.
item.description:
According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), as reported by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, industry, construction and energy suppliers together produced 0.7% more in September than in August. Handelsblatt adds that economists surveyed by Reuters had expected stagnation, that August growth was revised to 1.0% from a preliminary 2.0% because construction companies supplied further information from their VAT declarations, and that output in the third quarter was 0.4% lower than in the second. Car production rose 17.1% on the month and pharmaceuticals 8.0% after two weaker months, while construction fell 2.6%, mechanical engineering 6.5% and energy production 1.2%. Industrial production excluding energy and construction rose 1.7%, with investment goods up 3.0%, consumer goods up 0.8% and intermediate goods up 0.1%. Euronews gives output 0.4% higher than a year earlier; that is a different measure from the quarterly figure. The rows give no reason for the jump in car output, no share of cars in the total and no breakdown of construction.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report one month of production and show a rise that rests mainly on cars and pharmaceuticals. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, month-to-month swings in car output are large and the quarterly figure of minus 0.4% suggests that the September rise did not make up the earlier weakness. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher car output supports demand from vehicle makers and their suppliers, a fall in construction output points to weaker demand for building materials, and the 0.1% rise in intermediate goods, the category that includes materials such as chemicals, is small; the rows give no figures for adhesives or their raw materials. Points that may be worth considering include the October production data, revisions to the September figures and the construction output series.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Handelsblatt | Euronews

item.title: The three big German carmakers' annual deliveries in China fell by about a third to 3.87 million between 2019 and 2025, and, according to the China Passenger Car Association, Chinese carmakers' domestic share rose from 37.8% to 65.3%.
item.description:
The Bangkok Post reports that the annual vehicle deliveries in China of the big three German carmakers fell by about a third to 3.87 million between 2019 and 2025, and that, according to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), the share of Chinese carmakers in their home market rose from 37.8% to 65.3% over the same period. It adds that Volkswagen posted a loss of EUR 5.8 billion for the three months to the end of September, mainly because of its declining fortunes in China, and that up to 120,000 jobs could be cut at Volkswagen by the end of the decade; the row does not say how many of those jobs relate to China. The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung describes the situation as an existential crisis for Volkswagen, Mercedes and BMW in China: Mercedes and Volkswagen have significantly written down the value of their China businesses and report red figures there for the first time, BMW does not report China separately, and Volkswagen has built a second Wolfsburg in Hefei and is launching dozens of new models. The rows give no deliveries for 2026, no split of the 3.87 million by brand, no amounts for the write-downs or the China losses, and the two endpoints are six years apart.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report deliveries, a market share and company results, and the characterisation of an existential crisis is the newspaper's. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, lower deliveries by German carmakers in China reduce the volume of materials those plants buy, and a shift of the market to Chinese brands can move material specification and sourcing towards Chinese supply chains. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle output and the design of new models set the demand for bonding and sealing materials, and where a model is built and by which group affects which suppliers are qualified; the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the three groups' next quarterly results, CPCA monthly data and announcements on capacity or model launches in China.

Bangkok Post | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: The European Commission conditionally approved the proposed merger of equals between AkzoNobel and Axalta after they agreed to sell AkzoNobel's European vehicle refinish business, with closing expected in early 2027 subject to pending approvals.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that the European Commission granted conditional approval to the proposed all-stock merger of equals between Akzo Nobel N.V. and Axalta Coating Systems Ltd., which the row describes as creating a premier global coatings company. The condition is a targeted remedy: AkzoNobel divests its European vehicle refinish business. The row says the commitments remove the horizontal overlap between their activities in the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom and Switzerland, that the Commission identified no other competition issues in any other market, and that the outcome preserves the same level of competition and customer choice in vehicle refinish coatings in Europe. The transaction is expected to close in early 2027, subject to pending regulatory approvals. The row does not say whether its wording is the companies' or the Commission's. The row gives no deal value, no sales or earnings of the business to be sold, no buyer, no list of the approvals still pending and no statement from the Commission itself or from customers and competitors.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a regulatory decision and a remedy described by the companies, not data on market shares. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a divestiture limited to European vehicle refinish suggests that the competition concern was concentrated in that product line, and a merger of two large coatings groups combines suppliers that sell to car, building and industrial customers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, coatings and adhesive producers often serve the same customers and buy overlapping raw materials such as resins and solvents, so a larger coatings group can change purchasing scale and customer negotiations in those areas; the row gives no figures on any overlap with adhesives. Points that may be worth considering include the remaining regulatory approvals, the identity of the buyer of the refinish business and statements on integration plans.

MarketScreener
